name: Red yeast rice
short: Case reports: life-threatening muscle breakdown, kidney injury needing dialysis, liver injury. Japan survey: kidney injury in 192 on specific tablets, 87% still impaired (cause unproven).
text: In a nationwide survey of Japanese nephrologists, after kidney injury was linked in late 2023 to early 2024 to specific red yeast rice tablets, 94.1% of 192 affected patients had a low estimated glomerular filtration rate (under 60 ml/min/1.73m2), laboratory findings showed features of Fanconi syndrome (a disorder of the kidney tubules), and biopsies showed mainly tubulointerstitial changes (tubulointerstitial nephritis in 50%, tubular necrosis in 32%); Fanconi-related measures improved after the product was stopped and treatment given, but 87% still had a filtration rate under 60 at the last observation. The authors say citrinin, a known kidney toxin of red yeast rice, was not produced by the implicated strains, and that further research is needed to establish definitive causal relationships. Red yeast rice contains monacolin K, which one case report describes as identical to lovastatin (a statin medicine). Case reports describe rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown) in a 50-year-old woman who had started eating red yeast rice without telling her clinicians, and myopathy with a raised creatine phosphokinase level in a middle-aged man that resolved when he stopped the product and recurred when he resumed it; a third case report describes rhabdomyolysis in a stable kidney-transplant recipient who took a herbal mixture containing red yeast rice, which resolved when the product was stopped and which the authors postulated came from an interaction between cyclosporine (ciclosporin) and these compounds through the cytochrome P450 system. Case reports also describe liver injury. A 64-year-old woman had acute hepatitis 6 weeks after starting a red yeast rice supplement; infectious, toxic and autoimmune causes were ruled out, a liver biopsy was consistent with drug-induced liver injury, and her liver enzymes fell after she stopped it and was given intravenous methylprednisolone. A 62-year-old woman had mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic acute hepatitis, rated highly probable drug-induced liver injury (her autoimmune liver tests were positive), and her bilirubin and liver enzymes gradually fell after she stopped the product. A healthy 65-year-old man was admitted to hospital with acute kidney impairment, hepatitis and rhabdomyolysis, in a report titled as presuming red yeast rice to be the cause of acute kidney and liver failure. In a life-threatening case, rhabdomyolysis with severe hyperkalaemia (high blood potassium), weakness of all four limbs (tetraparesis) and liver injury needed intensive care; an over-the-counter supplement containing red yeast rice was identified as the sole possible trigger, and the patient regained full function. In a report of two people with kidney injury after taking a functional food containing red yeast rice, one, who had diabetes, had severe kidney injury, needed haemodialysis for more than 2 weeks and recovered kidney function after the product was stopped (his biopsy also showed changes consistent with diabetic kidney disease); the other was diagnosed with Fanconi syndrome, and her kidney function returned to baseline 35 days after stopping. An analysis of two US Food and Drug Administration adverse-event reporting systems found disproportionately high reporting of serious muscle and liver injuries with red yeast rice products: 5 cases of liver disorders in one system, in which red yeast rice was mainly reported as a concomitant agent (reporting odds ratio 13.71), and 27 cases of rhabdomyolysis or myopathy in the other, in which it was mainly recorded as a suspect agent (8.44); the authors note recognised limitations of these data. A 2018 letter with no abstract is titled as reporting an exacerbation of myasthenia gravis after red yeast rice use. A review of US Food and Drug Administration reporting systems and published case reports found very few cases of rhabdomyolysis or severe acute hepatitis and judged them extremely rare compared with statins; the same review notes that the European Food Safety Authority concluded that monacolins from red yeast rice raise significant safety concerns at 10 mg/day and that individual cases of serious adverse effects have been reported at intakes as low as 3 mg/day. On the other side, a meta-analysis of 53 randomised trials (8535 subjects) of red yeast rice alone or combined with other nutraceutical compounds found no increased risk of musculoskeletal disorders (odds ratio 0.94) and a reduced risk of other adverse events and of serious adverse events compared with control, and a 2015 meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials, most with low-quality safety assessment, reported an incidence of liver and kidney injury of 0 to 5%, with no difference in risk between treatment and control groups; its title states that the safety of red yeast rice is uncertain. An umbrella review of 15 meta-analyses (80% rated critically low confidence) found that 5 of 61 associations indicated an increased risk, related to uric acid and the liver enzymes ALT and AST, and judged the credibility of the evidence not high. The only medicine interaction named in the cited sources is with cyclosporine, in one case report.
